title: Hotspot Handling
description: Tackle the celebrity problem with key salting, scatter-gather patterns, Slack's channel sharding story, and production hotspot monitoring.

segments.text: No matter how clever your partition strategy, some keys are just more popular than others. When Justin Bieber posts an Instagram photo, the partition holding his follower list handles ten million fan-out operations while other partitions handle ten. This is the celebrity problem, and it will break your system if you don't plan for it.

Hot partitions emerge from two sources. First, naturally skewed data: a viral tweet, a popular product, a celebrity user. Second, temporal patterns: Black Friday sales hammering the 'orders' partition, or a news event causing everyone to search the same term. Hash partitioning distributes keys evenly, but it can't distribute traffic for a single key.

Key salting is the primary weapon. Instead of partition key 'celebrity_123', you create 'celebrity_123_0' through 'celebrity_123_9'. Ten keys, spreading across ten partitions. Writes pick a random suffix. Reads must query all ten suffixes and aggregate. You've traded read complexity for write distribution. Instagram uses this exact pattern for follower counts.
segments.thought_prompt: How would you choose the number of salt suffixes? What happens if you pick too many?

segments.text: Salting forces scatter-gather on reads. You query all salt partitions in parallel and combine results. For counters, you sum. For lists, you merge. The latency is dominated by the slowest partition response, the tail latency problem. With ten partitions, you're almost guaranteed to hit the ninety-ninth percentile on at least one.

Slack's channel sharding is a masterclass in hotspot handling. Their largest customers have channels with fifty thousand members sending messages simultaneously. They shard message storage by channel ID, but channels themselves vary wildly in activity. A channel with three people and a channel with fifty thousand can't share resources.

Slack's solution: they detect hot channels dynamically and isolate them to dedicated infrastructure. When a channel exceeds a throughput threshold, it gets promoted to its own shard with more resources. Think of it as automatic VIP treatment. The monitoring system identifies hotspots, and automation handles the migration with zero downtime.

You cannot fix what you cannot see. Production hotspot monitoring requires per-partition metrics: QPS, latency p99, CPU utilization, disk I/O. Set alerts when any partition exceeds two times the mean. DynamoDB adaptive capacity does this automatically, shifting capacity from cool partitions to hot ones in real time.

For write-heavy hotspots, another technique is local aggregation. Instead of writing every event to the hot partition immediately, buffer writes in memory and flush aggregated results periodically. Twitter does this for like counts: individual likes aggregate locally every few seconds, then one batched write updates the partition.
segments.thought_prompt: What's the risk of local aggregation if the aggregating node crashes before flushing?

segments.text: The best hotspot is one you prevent. Design your partition keys with your access patterns in mind. If you know certain entities will be hot, build salting in from the start. If traffic is temporal, use composite keys that spread time-based writes. And always, always have a runbook for when a partition goes hot unexpectedly.

Hotspot handling is where theoretical partitioning meets messy production reality. Your partition strategy might be perfect for uniform data, but the real world isn't uniform. Plan for celebrities, plan for viral events, plan for the unexpected. The partition that melts is always the one you didn't plan for.
